title: Jaw Pain After Drinking: Teeth Grinding, TMJ, and Other Causes
excerpt: Why your jaw or teeth hurt after drinking: night-time grinding, TMJ flare-ups, dry mouth, salivary glands, and the rare heart warning sign. What helps and when to see a doctor.
metaDescription: Why your jaw or teeth hurt after drinking alcohol: grinding, TMJ, dry mouth, and salivary glands. What helps, and when jaw pain needs a doctor.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most jaw pain after a night of drinking comes from your own muscles. Alcohol makes many people clench and grind their teeth in their sleep, and a few hours of that leaves the jaw joint and chewing muscles sore and stiff the next morning, sometimes with aching teeth or a headache at the temples. Dehydration, a dry mouth, acidic or sugary drinks, and vomiting can add to it. That kind of soreness usually fades within a day or two and responds to rest, soft food, water, and warmth.

A smaller set of causes deserves more attention: a swollen, painful salivary gland under the jaw or in front of the ear, a tooth that throbs or a swollen gum (possible infection), and, rarely, jaw pain that is really coming from the heart. This guide walks through each cause, how to tell them apart, what helps, and when to see a doctor or dentist.

> **When to see a doctor.** This article is general information, not medical advice. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away if** jaw pain comes with chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, lightheadedness, or pain spreading to the arm, neck, or back. Jaw pain can be a heart attack symptom, especially in women and older adults, and drinking does not rule that out. **See a doctor or dentist soon if** you have swelling in your face, under your jaw, or in front of your ear; fever; a bad taste or pus in your mouth; a tooth that throbs or is sensitive to biting; trouble opening your mouth or swallowing; a jaw that locks; or pain that lasts more than a few days or keeps returning every time you drink. **If you vomited blood or something that looks like coffee grounds**, get medical care the same day.

## Why Does My Jaw Hurt After Drinking Alcohol?

The jaw is not one thing. When people say "my jaw hurts," the pain can come from:

- **The chewing muscles** (the masseter at the angle of your jaw and the temporalis at your temples). These are the most common source after drinking.
- **The jaw joint**, the temporomandibular joint (TMJ), which sits just in front of each ear.
- **The teeth and gums.**
- **The salivary glands**: the parotid glands in front of the ears and the submandibular glands under the jaw.
- **Something farther away** that refers pain to the jaw, such as the sinuses, the ears, or, rarely, the heart.

Alcohol can affect several of these at once. Here are the main causes, from most to least common for a typical social drinker.

## Teeth Grinding and Clenching (Sleep Bruxism)

Grinding or clenching your teeth while asleep is called sleep bruxism. Research on bruxism has repeatedly linked it with alcohol, along with smoking, caffeine, stress, and some sleep problems. Studies of people who drink more tend to report more grinding, and sleep-lab work suggests drinking in the evening can increase grinding episodes that night. The link is an association rather than a precise dose and effect, and plenty of people grind without drinking, but the pattern is common enough that dentists routinely ask about alcohol when they see worn teeth.

Why alcohol might do this is not fully settled. The most likely explanation is the way it disrupts sleep. Alcohol makes you sleepy at first, but as your body clears it during the second half of the night, sleep becomes lighter and more broken, with more brief awakenings. Grinding episodes tend to cluster around these micro-arousals. Alcohol also affects brain chemicals involved in muscle control during sleep, and it can relax the airway, which may make snoring and breathing pauses worse. Some researchers think clenching can be partly a response to a narrowed airway. (Our guide to [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains the rebound effect in more detail.)

**What grinding-related jaw pain feels like:**

- A dull ache or tightness on both sides of the jaw, worst right after waking.
- Tender muscles at the angle of the jaw or at the temples when you press on them.
- A tension-type headache around the temples or forehead.
- Teeth that feel sore, "loose," or sensitive to cold, often several teeth at once rather than one.
- Sometimes a partner who heard you grinding.

This kind of soreness usually eases over the day and fades within a day or two. If it happens every time you drink, though, it is worth bringing up with your dentist. Repeated heavy grinding can wear down enamel, crack fillings, and strain the jaw joint over time.

## TMJ Pain After Drinking

TMJ disorders (often written TMD) are problems with the jaw joint and the muscles that move it. They cause pain in front of the ear, clicking or popping when you open your mouth, limited opening, and sometimes a jaw that briefly catches or locks.

Alcohol does not cause TMJ disorders directly, but people who already have a sensitive jaw joint often notice flare-ups after drinking. The likely reasons are the ones above: more clenching and grinding at night, plus poor-quality sleep, which makes pain feel worse in general. A few other drinking-night habits load the joint too:

- Talking, laughing, and singing loudly for hours.
- Chewing ice, gum, or tough bar snacks.
- Yawning wide when you're tired.
- Sleeping in an awkward position, face down or with your jaw pressed into a pillow or arm.
- Vomiting, which forces the jaw wide open and tenses the neck and face.

If you have known TMJ trouble and it flares after drinking, the usual TMJ self-care applies: soft food for a few days, no gum, small bites, warmth on the sore muscles, gentle jaw stretches, and avoiding wide yawns. If clicking turns into locking, or you can't open your mouth normally, see a dentist or doctor.

## Why Do My Teeth Hurt After Drinking?

Teeth that ache after drinking usually point to one of these:

**1. Grinding and clenching.** As above. Pressure from clenching makes teeth and the ligaments that hold them in the jaw sore, so several teeth feel tender when you bite.

**2. Sensitivity to cold, sugar, or acid.** Many drinks are cold, sugary, acidic, or all three. Wine, especially white wine, is quite acidic. Cocktails often add citrus juice, syrups, or soda. Hard seltzers and mixers are usually carbonated, and carbonation adds acidity. If you have worn enamel, exposed roots from receding gums, or a small cavity, these drinks can trigger a sharp, short zing of pain. That sensitivity can feel worse after a night of sipping because your teeth spent hours bathed in acid.

**3. A dry mouth.** Saliva protects teeth by washing away sugar and neutralizing acid. Alcohol makes you pass more urine and can leave you mildly dehydrated, and many people breathe through their mouth when they sleep after drinking. Less saliva means acid and sugar sit on your teeth longer, and a dry mouth can make existing sensitivity feel worse.

**4. Sinus congestion.** Alcohol can cause a stuffy nose in some people, partly because it widens blood vessels and partly because some drinks (especially wine and beer) contain histamine and other compounds that bother sensitive people. The roots of the upper back teeth sit right under the maxillary sinuses. When those sinuses are swollen or full, the upper teeth can ache, often on both sides, and the ache gets worse when you bend over.

**5. A dental problem that drinking made you notice.** A cavity, cracked tooth, failing filling, or early infection can be quiet until something cold, sweet, or hard sets it off. **If one tooth throbs, wakes you up, hurts when you bite down on it, or your gum or face is swelling, see a dentist.** That points to the tooth itself, not to the alcohol, and tooth infections need treatment.

**What helps teeth that hurt after drinking:** rinse with water after drinking and between drinks, wait about 30 to 60 minutes before brushing after acidic drinks so you don't scrub softened enamel, use a soft brush and a toothpaste for sensitive teeth, and avoid very cold or sugary food for a day. If the pain doesn't settle within a few days, have it checked.

## Dehydration, Dry Mouth, and Muscle Soreness

Alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally tells your kidneys to hold onto water, so you pass more fluid than you take in. Mild dehydration is one reason the morning after feels rough. It makes your mouth dry, can make muscles feel achy and tight, and may contribute to headaches. (Our article on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) goes into how much it actually matters.)

For the jaw specifically, dehydration probably doesn't cause pain by itself so much as make other problems worse: a dry mouth makes teeth more sensitive, and thick, slow-moving saliva sets up the salivary-gland problems described next. Body-wide achiness after drinking is common too, and our guide to [body aches after drinking](/never-hungover/body-aches-after-drinking) covers the general causes.

## Salivary Gland Pain After Drinking

You have three pairs of major salivary glands: the parotids (in front of each ear, over the angle of the jaw), the submandibulars (under the jawbone toward the back), and the sublinguals (under the tongue). Pain or swelling in these areas can feel like "jaw pain," but it behaves differently from muscle soreness.

**Salivary stones (sialolithiasis).** Small mineral stones can form inside a salivary duct, most often the submandibular gland under the jaw. When the duct is blocked, saliva backs up. The classic sign is pain and swelling under the jaw that **comes on when you eat or even think about food**, then slowly settles over an hour or two. Dehydration is a known risk factor because thicker saliva moves more slowly. A night of drinking doesn't create a stone, but if you already have one, a dry, dehydrated mouth can make a flare more likely. Sucking on sour sweets, drinking plenty of water, gentle massage of the gland toward the mouth, and warmth sometimes help a small stone pass. Stones that keep causing trouble are treated by a doctor or an ear, nose, and throat (ENT) specialist.

**Salivary gland infection (sialadenitis).** If a gland becomes infected, it gets painful, swollen, warm, and tender, and you may notice a bad taste or pus in the mouth, fever, or redness of the skin over the gland. Dehydration and a dry mouth are risk factors. **This needs a doctor, usually the same day or next day**, because it often needs antibiotics.

**Swollen parotid glands with regular heavy drinking (sialadenosis).** Long-term heavy drinking is a recognized cause of painless enlargement of the parotid glands, which makes the face look fuller in front of the ears and along the jaw. It is usually painless, develops over months or years, and isn't caused by one night out. If you notice persistent swelling of both cheeks or the angle of your jaw, see a doctor so they can look at the cause. If you're also wondering about general puffiness the morning after, see our guide to [face bloating after drinking](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating).

**How to tell gland pain from muscle pain:** gland pain tends to sit under the jaw or in front of the ear over a lump you can feel, gets worse with eating, and may come with visible swelling. Muscle pain is usually on both sides, feels like tightness or fatigue, is worst in the morning, and gets better as the day goes on.

## Vomiting and Jaw Pain

Being sick after drinking is hard on the jaw. Vomiting forces the mouth wide open and tightens the muscles of the face, neck, and jaw, and repeated retching can leave them sore the next day. Stomach acid also coats the teeth. If you vomited, rinse your mouth with water (or water with a little baking soda), wait before brushing, and drink fluids slowly to rehydrate.

Two things are worth knowing. First, if you notice blood or material that looks like coffee grounds in your vomit, get medical care the same day; our guide on [vomiting blood after drinking](/never-hungover/vomiting-blood-after-drinking) explains why. Second, vomiting a lot in a short time while very drunk is a sign of dangerous intoxication. If someone can't stay awake, is confused, is breathing slowly or irregularly, or is vomiting while barely conscious, call 911.

## Jaw Pain That Could Be Your Heart

This is uncommon but important. Pain from the heart doesn't always show up in the chest. It can be felt in the jaw, neck, shoulder, arm, or back, and jaw pain is one of the symptoms more often reported by women. Angina (heart pain from reduced blood flow) is often triggered by exertion, stress, cold, or a heavy meal, and heavy drinking can strain the heart in several ways, including triggering irregular heart rhythms in some people.

**Treat jaw pain as a possible heart problem and call 911 if it:**

- Comes with chest pain, pressure, squeezing, or tightness.
- Comes with shortness of breath, cold sweats, nausea, lightheadedness, or unusual tiredness.
- Spreads to or from the arm, neck, shoulder, or back.
- Comes on with physical effort and eases with rest.
- Doesn't change when you press on your jaw muscles or move your jaw.

Muscle and joint jaw pain usually changes when you chew, open wide, or press on the sore spot. Heart-related jaw pain usually doesn't. If you're not sure, don't wait it out to see if it's "just a hangover." If your main symptom is a pounding or fast heartbeat after drinking, our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking) explains common causes and red flags.

## Other, Less Common Causes

**Ear problems.** The jaw joint sits right next to the ear canal, so ear infections and jaw joint pain are easy to confuse in both directions.

**Injury.** Falls, bumping into things, or a knock to the face are more likely when you're drunk, and the pain may not register until the next day. If your bite feels "off," your jaw is badly swollen or bruised, you can't open or close your mouth normally, or you have numbness in the lip or chin, see a doctor promptly, as these can be signs of a fracture or dislocation.

**Nerve pain.** Trigeminal neuralgia causes brief, severe, electric-shock pains in the face and jaw, often set off by touch, chewing, or talking. It isn't caused by alcohol, but it can be mistaken for a tooth or jaw problem. A doctor or dentist can sort this out.

**Pain in a lymph node after drinking.** A very rare but well-described sign: some people with Hodgkin lymphoma feel pain in swollen lymph nodes, sometimes in the neck just below the jaw, shortly after drinking alcohol. This is rare, and almost everyone with jaw pain after drinking does not have it. But if you have a firm, swollen lump in your neck that hurts specifically after drinking, especially with night sweats, fever, or weight loss you can't explain, see a doctor.

## How to Relieve Jaw Pain the Morning After

For ordinary muscle soreness from clenching, grinding, or a long night of talking:

1. **Drink water.** Rehydrate steadily over the morning. An electrolyte drink is fine if you also feel run down, but plain water does most of the work.
2. **Apply warmth.** A warm, damp cloth on the jaw muscles for 10 to 15 minutes a few times a day can ease tightness. Some people prefer a cold pack wrapped in a cloth for the first few hours if the area feels swollen.
3. **Rest your jaw.** Eat soft food (eggs, yogurt, soup, oatmeal, bananas), cut food into small pieces, and skip gum, ice, crusty bread, and chewy snacks for a day or two.
4. **Gentle massage and stretching.** Use your fingertips to massage the muscles at the angle of the jaw and the temples in small circles. Then slowly open and close your mouth within a comfortable range.
5. **Keep your teeth apart.** During the day, many people clench without noticing. The resting position is "lips together, teeth apart, tongue resting on the roof of the mouth." Checking this a few times an hour helps.
6. **Consider a pain reliever, carefully.** An over-the-counter pain reliever can help, but both common types carry label warnings for people who have 3 or more drinks a day. Ibuprofen and naproxen are harder on the stomach, which alcohol already irritates; acetaminophen (Tylenol) is processed by the liver and can be risky after heavy drinking. Take any of them with food and water, at the label dose, once the alcohol has cleared. Our guides to [ibuprofen and alcohol](/never-hungover/ibuprofen-and-alcohol) and [Advil vs. Tylenol for a hangover](/never-hungover/advil-or-tylenol-for-hangover) explain the trade-offs. Ask a pharmacist if you take other medicines.

If the pain is coming from a tooth, a salivary gland, or swelling, home care isn't enough. See a dentist or doctor.

## How to Prevent Jaw Pain When You Drink

- **Drink less and stop earlier.** Fewer drinks, finished a few hours before bed, gives your body time to clear alcohol before sleep, which likely means less of the late-night rebound that seems to drive grinding.
- **Alternate with water.** A glass of water between drinks slows your pace, keeps your mouth wetter, and limits dehydration.
- **Mind acidic and sugary drinks.** If your teeth are sensitive, cut back on citrus cocktails, sweet mixers, and carbonated drinks, or drink them with a straw and rinse with water afterward.
- **Skip the ice chewing and late-night gum.**
- **Wear your night guard.** If your dentist has already made you a night guard for grinding, nights you drink are the nights it matters most. If you don't have one and you keep waking up with a sore jaw, ask your dentist whether one makes sense. Custom guards fitted by a dentist usually fit better than store-bought ones.
- **Manage stress.** Stress and anxiety are among the strongest links to clenching. If you wake up anxious and tense after drinking, our [hangxiety guide](/never-hungover/hangxiety-complete-guide-2026-supplements-research) covers why that happens and what helps.
- **Sleep on your back or side,** not with your jaw pressed into a pillow or your arm.

Some people also ask about magnesium for muscle tension and grinding. The evidence for magnesium preventing bruxism is limited, so there is no good evidence that it will stop your jaw pain. Our page on [magnesium and alcohol](/never-hungover/magnesium-and-alcohol) covers what the research does and doesn't show.

## Where Does DHM Fit In?

DHM (dihydromyricetin) is a plant compound that many people take before or while drinking. Research, mostly in animals with limited human data, suggests it may affect how the body handles alcohol and how alcohol acts on the brain. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents teeth grinding or jaw pain, and it won't fix a tooth problem, a blocked salivary gland, or anything heart-related.

Its possible role here is indirect: if you're trying to feel better overall the morning after, some people find DHM part of a routine that also includes eating, drinking water, and moderating how much they drink. If you want to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how much to take and when, and our broader guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence. No supplement replaces drinking less.

## The Bottom Line

Jaw pain after drinking is usually a muscle problem: alcohol disrupts your sleep and many people clench and grind as a result, leaving the jaw and teeth sore the next morning. Dehydration, a dry mouth, acidic drinks, and vomiting can add to it. Water, warmth, soft food, rest, and drinking less and earlier usually take care of it.

Pay attention when the pattern doesn't fit. One throbbing tooth, swelling under the jaw or in front of the ear, fever, pus, a jaw that won't open, or pain that keeps returning are reasons to see a dentist or doctor. Jaw pain with chest pressure, shortness of breath, or sweating is a reason to call 911.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Why does my jaw hurt after drinking alcohol?**

The most common reason is clenching or grinding your teeth during sleep. Alcohol disrupts sleep in the second half of the night, and bruxism (grinding) has been linked with drinking in several studies. That leaves the jaw muscles and joint sore in the morning. Dehydration, dry mouth, acidic drinks, vomiting, and a flare of an existing TMJ problem can also contribute. Less often, the pain comes from a tooth, a salivary gland, or the heart.

**Why do my teeth hurt after drinking?**

Usually because of grinding and clenching overnight, which makes several teeth feel sore when you bite. Cold, sugary, acidic, or carbonated drinks can also trigger sensitivity if you have worn enamel, exposed roots, or a small cavity, and a dry mouth makes that worse. Sinus congestion can make the upper back teeth ache. If one tooth throbs, hurts when you bite on it, or your gum is swelling, see a dentist, because that suggests a dental problem rather than the alcohol itself.

**Does alcohol make you grind your teeth?**

It can. Studies have found that people who drink more report more teeth grinding, and drinking in the evening has been linked with more grinding episodes that night. The likely reason is the lighter, more broken sleep that follows as your body clears alcohol. It's an association rather than a guarantee, and plenty of people grind for other reasons, such as stress. If you regularly wake up with a sore jaw after drinking, ask your dentist about a night guard.

**Can alcohol make TMJ worse?**

It can trigger flare-ups in people who already have a sensitive jaw joint, mainly through more clenching and grinding at night and poorer sleep. Loud talking, chewing ice, wide yawning, and vomiting add strain. Soft food, warmth, gentle stretching, and avoiding gum for a few days usually help. See a dentist or doctor if your jaw locks, you can't open your mouth normally, or the pain doesn't settle.

**Why does the area under my jaw hurt after drinking?**

Pain and swelling under the jaw that gets worse when you eat can be a salivary stone blocking the submandibular gland's duct, and dehydration makes stones more likely to flare. If the area is red, warm, very tender, or you have a fever or a bad taste in your mouth, the gland may be infected and you should see a doctor promptly. A painful swollen lymph node after drinking is a rare sign worth getting checked.

**Can jaw pain after drinking be a heart attack?**

Rarely, yes. Heart pain can be felt in the jaw, neck, arm, or back, and jaw pain is a more common heart symptom in women. Call 911 if jaw pain comes with chest pressure, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or lightheadedness, or if it comes on with effort and doesn't change when you move or press on your jaw. Don't assume it's a hangover.

**How long does jaw pain from drinking last?**

Muscle soreness from grinding or clenching usually eases over the day and fades within one to two days. If it lasts longer than a few days, keeps coming back every time you drink, or comes with swelling, fever, or a single painful tooth, see a dentist or doctor.

**What is the fastest way to relieve a sore jaw after drinking?**

Drink water, put a warm damp cloth on the jaw muscles for 10 to 15 minutes, eat soft food, massage the sore muscles gently, and keep your teeth apart during the day. An over-the-counter pain reliever taken with food and at the label dose can help once the alcohol has cleared, but check the alcohol warnings on the label and ask a pharmacist if you drink heavily or take other medicines.

**Can DHM prevent jaw pain from drinking?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents teeth grinding or jaw pain. Some people take it as part of a routine to feel better the morning after drinking, but the research is mostly from animal studies. Drinking less, finishing earlier, staying hydrated, and wearing a night guard if you grind are the more direct steps.
